Small area estimation with a Fay-Herriot model

Source: vignettes/small-area-estimation.Rmd
small-area-estimation.Rmd

Small area estimation often starts from a survey that gives a direct estimate for each area, such as a district or a county, with a variance computed from the survey design. In the area-level model of Fay and Herriot (1979), the direct estimates play the part of a multisite trial’s site estimates. Each direct estimate is normal around the area’s true value, with its sampling variance vjv_j, and the true values are normal around a regression on area covariates, with variance στ2\sigma_\tau^2. Under this model, the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of an area’s true value pulls the direct estimate toward the regression prediction and keeps the weight

Sj=στ2στ2+vj S_j = \frac{\sigma_\tau^2}{\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j}

on the area’s own estimate. These weights are poolinfo’s site reliabilities. In this vignette we compute their diagnostics for a set of simulated areas under two mean models, and we set the posterior means beside the empirical BLUP (EBLUP). We report the informativeness II, the mean reliability S‾\bar S, the dispersion HH, the logit variance VV and the concentration count JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} of each fit, as vignette("poolinfo") defines them.

In the small area literature the same quantities go by other letters. Much of the Fay-Herriot literature writes AA for στ2\sigma_\tau^2 and DjD_j for vjv_j, and Rao and Molina (2015) write

  • σv2\sigma_v^2 for στ2\sigma_\tau^2, the variance of the true values around the regression;
  • ψj\psi_j for vjv_j, the sampling variance of area jj’s direct estimate;
  • γj\gamma_j for SjS_j, the weight on the area’s direct estimate.
library(poolinfo)

Simulated areas

We simulate areas whose survey samples differ widely in size. Each direct estimate is a mean, with a design effect of 1.5 on its variance, and the true area means depend on a covariate x, such as a standardized measure of poverty from administrative records.

set.seed(20261014)
J <- 150
n <- pmax(8, round(exp(rnorm(J, log(60), 0.9))))
x <- rnorm(J)
truth <- 0.2 + 0.4 * x + rnorm(J, sd = 0.15)
se <- sqrt(1.5 / n)
areas <- data.frame(area = sprintf("A%03d", seq_len(J)), n = n, x = x,
                    estimate = rnorm(J, truth, se), se = se)
summary(areas$n)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    8.00   30.25   63.50   81.01  107.00  453.00

Across the 150 areas, samples range from 8 to 453 respondents, with a median of 63.5. In a real application, estimate and se would be each area’s direct estimate and its design-based standard error. Like the analysis of a multisite trial, the Fay-Herriot model treats the sampling variances as known, although they are estimated from the same small samples. In practice the direct variances are often smoothed first, for example with a generalized variance function, before they enter the model (Rao and Molina 2015). Whatever noise the variances carry passes into the diagnostics. VV is the variance of the logarithms of the vjv_j, so independent errors in the estimated variances tend to raise it, and they spread the reliabilities further apart. Our simulation uses the true variances, which stand in for smoothed ones.

A common mean and a regression mean

We fit the posterior twice, first with a common mean for all the areas and then with the covariate in the mean, as in the Fay-Herriot model. mean_model takes a one-sided formula, and its variables are looked up in data.

common <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = area, data = areas)
regression <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = area,
                                    data = areas, mean_model = ~ x)
compare_profiles(`common mean` = common, `mean model ~ x` = regression)
#> Comparison of 2 analyses
#> Intervals are central posterior intervals.
#> Each analysis is conditional on its own standard errors.
#> 
#>   analysis        J    informativeness I     mean reliability
#>   common mean     150  0.891 [0.864, 0.915]  0.864
#>   mean model ~ x  150  0.532 [0.428, 0.629]  0.528
#> 
#>   analysis        dispersion H             concentration count J_eff
#>   common mean     0.0378 [0.0309, 0.0451]  148.1
#>   mean model ~ x  0.0850 [0.0813, 0.0859]  132.9

With a common mean, the between-area standard deviation includes everything that the covariate explains. Its posterior mean is 0.467 and II is 0.89, so the model would move an area with the geometric-mean standard error only about 11% of the way toward the common mean. With the covariate, στ\sigma_\tau is the standard deviation of the true values around the regression line, 0.174, and II falls to 0.53. Because the Fay-Herriot predictor shrinks toward the regression prediction, the second profile is the one that describes it. When you report the diagnostics of an area-level model, report them for the mean model that your predictor uses.

Both fits have the same logit variance, V=0.73V = 0.73, because VV depends on the standard errors alone. Their dispersions differ (0.038 with the common mean and 0.085 with the covariate), because the leading term of HH, I(1−I)V/2I(1 - I)V/2, is largest at I=1/2I = 1/2.

We print the fit with the covariate, which lists the posterior of the regression coefficients beside the diagnostics.

regression
#> Reliability profile of 150 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(x'beta, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the coefficients of the mean model and on sigma_tau
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#>                              mean     95% interval
#>   informativeness I          0.532    0.428    0.629
#>   mean reliability           0.528    0.439    0.612
#>   dispersion H               0.0850   0.0813   0.0859
#>   concentration count J_eff  132.9    127.2    137.8    of 150
#>   logit variance V           0.735    (fixed by the standard errors)
#>   sigma_tau                  0.174    0.140    0.211
#>   coefficient (Intercept)    0.200    0.161    0.239
#>   coefficient x              0.439    0.400    0.479
#> 
#>   Pr(I > 0.5)                0.735
#>   I at E(sigma_tau^2)        0.537

Its intercept and slope have posterior means of 0.200 and 0.439. Each area counts once in the diagnostics, whether its sample has 8 respondents or 453.

Concentration of the reliability

A direct estimate’s variance here is proportional to 1/n1/n, so the 57-fold range of the sample sizes carries over to the variances. plot_concentration() shows how the total reliability ∑jSj\sum_j S_j accumulates over the areas, from the most reliable one down.

plot_concentration(regression, label_top = 0)

At a quarter of the areas the curve reaches 36%, so the most reliable quarter carries that proportion of the total reliability, although it has 55% of the total precision, the sum of the 1/vj1/v_j. A reliability cannot exceed 1, and the most precise areas, with reliabilities up to 0.90, cannot carry reliability in proportion to their precision. So the total reliability is spread more evenly over the areas than the precision is, and the concentration count of 132.9 of 150 puts that spread in one number.

The areas

We plot each direct estimate beside the posterior mean of its area’s true value, with the areas ordered by reliability. With this many areas the plot has no labels, and we name its horizontal axis after what it shows.

plot_pooling(regression, order = "reliability") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Area mean")

The least reliable areas are at the bottom. Their posterior intervals are much shorter than the intervals of their direct estimates (for the least reliable area, 38% as long), and their posterior means lie away from the direct estimates, toward the regression predictions. Toward the top the two intervals of an area nearly coincide, and for the most reliable area the posterior interval is 95% as long as the direct one.

site_table() gives the numbers behind the plot. We add each area’s regression prediction, the intercept plus the slope times x at their posterior means, and show the three areas with the smallest standard errors and the three with the largest.

coefs <- subset(profile_summary(regression), grepl("^coef_", quantity))$mean
tab <- site_table(regression)
tab$prediction <- coefs[1] + coefs[2] * areas$x
tab <- tab[order(tab$se), c("site", "estimate", "prediction", "se",
                            "reliability", "effect")]
print(rbind(head(tab, 3), tail(tab, 3)), digits = 2)
#>     site estimate prediction    se reliability effect
#> 128 A128    0.095     -0.034 0.058        0.90  0.082
#> 137 A137   -0.228      0.131 0.063        0.88 -0.186
#> 2   A002   -0.074     -0.118 0.068        0.87 -0.080
#> 130 A130    0.849      0.579 0.408        0.15  0.620
#> 107 A107   -0.389     -0.582 0.433        0.14 -0.555
#> 120 A120    0.953      0.855 0.433        0.14  0.868

Each posterior mean lies between the area’s direct estimate and its prediction, about 1−Sj1 - S_j of the way from the first to the second. In the first three rows, with reliabilities of 0.86 and more, the posterior means stay near the direct estimates. In the last three, with reliabilities of 0.16 or less, they move most of the way to the predictions.

Posterior means and the EBLUP

The posterior means here come from the normal model with flat priors on the coefficients and on στ\sigma_\tau, averaged over the posterior of στ\sigma_\tau. In the usual Fay-Herriot predictor, the EBLUP, an estimate of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 such as the REML estimate goes into the BLUP instead (Rao and Molina 2015). metafor fits the same model by REML. Next we compute the profile at its estimate, and the largest difference between an EBLUP, from metafor::blup(), and the posterior mean of the same area.

fh <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, mods = ~ x, data = areas,
                   method = "REML")
reliability_profile(fh)
#> Reliability profile of 150 sites at sigma_tau = 0.172 (metafor REML estimate)
#> 
#>   informativeness I            0.529
#>   mean reliability             0.526
#>   dispersion H                 0.0858
#>   logit variance V             0.735
#>   concentration count J_eff    132.8 of 150
#> 
#> Site reliabilities range from 0.14 to 0.90.
max(abs(metafor::blup(fh)$pred - site_table(regression)$effect))
#> [1] 0.002484042

At the REML estimate, στ=0.172\sigma_\tau = 0.172 and I=0.529I = 0.529, against a posterior mean of 0.532 for II and a value of 0.537 at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2. With 150 areas the 95% posterior interval of στ\sigma_\tau runs from 0.140 to 0.211, so these three values of II lie within 0.009 of one another, and no EBLUP differs from its area’s posterior mean by more than 0.003. With few areas the posterior mean of II, its value at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 and its value at the REML estimate can be far apart, as vignette("posterior-summaries") shows for the eight schools.

References

Fay, Robert E., III, and Roger A. Herriot. 1979. “Estimates of Income for Small Places: An Application of James-Stein Procedures to Census Data.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 74 (366): 269–77. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1979.10482505.
Rao, J. N. K., and Isabel Molina. 2015. Small Area Estimation. 2nd ed. Wiley. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118735855.
